# vkernels — low-level CUDA kernels and communication primitives

`vkernels` is the kernel layer for [opentela](https://github.com/opentela-ai): hand-tuned
CUDA kernels and the communication primitives (collectives, overlap, topology) that sit
beside them. Everything ships with a **CPU reference implementation** so it can be unit-tested
and measured for coverage on machines **without a GPU**, and a CUDA implementation that is
compiled automatically when a CUDA toolkit is present.

> **Documentation in depth:** the [project wiki](https://github.com/opentela-ai/vkernels/wiki)
> distills the engineering knowledge — the roofline method, the kernel optimization ladder,
> occupancy/latency findings, cross-architecture lessons (MI300A vs GB10 vs MI250X), numerics
> and oracle contracts, LDS layout, CUDA-graph capture rules, debugging case files, and the
> per-kernel catalog with gaps to speed of light.

## Layout

```
vkernels/
├── pyproject.toml            # Python project (src/python/vkernels), managed with uv
├── uv.lock                   #   `uv sync` installs the `vkl` CLI + deps
├── src/c/                     # C++/CUDA sources (the kernel library)
│   └── vkernels/
│       ├── util/             # Span, error/status, logging, build annotations
│       ├── core/             # device, stream, allocator abstractions
│       ├── kernels/          # low-level CUDA kernels, each with a CPU oracle
│       │   ├── elementwise/  #   add, scale, relu, …
│       │   ├── reduce/       #   block/grid reduction
│       │   └── gemm/         #   tiled SGEMM
│       └── comm/             # communication optimisation
│           ├── topology.{hpp,cpp}   #   rank/world/peer discovery
│           ├── channel.{hpp,cpp}    #   transport abstraction + mock backend
│           ├── allreduce.{hpp,cpp,cu}#  ring all-reduce
│           ├── overlap.{hpp,cpp}    #   compute/communication overlap
│           └── pipeline_boundary.{hpp,cpp,cu} # graph-capturable PP boundary (#10)
├── tests/                    # C++ unit tests mirroring src/c/ (100% line coverage target)
│   ├── python/               #   Python tests (vkl CLI + bindings)
│   └── third_party/minitest.hpp     # dependency-free test harness
├── meta/                     # build support: cmake, scripts, docker, benchmarks
│   ├── cmake/                #   CMake helpers (CUDA, coverage, sanitizers, testing)
│   ├── scripts/              #   build / test / coverage / format helpers

│   │       ├── cli/          #     argparse CLI (`list`, `info`)
│   │       ├── torch_ops/    #     device-op kernels adopted from floe (see below)

│   └── rust/                 #   Rust bindings (workspace: `vkernels-sys` FFI + `vkernels` safe API)
```

# DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on A100 (sm80)

This repository contains a custom inference runtime for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on NVIDIA A100 GPUs. It keeps FP8 dense weights and packed FP4 MoE experts on GPU, uses Triton/CUDA kernels with BF16 tensor cores, and keeps the large Engram tables in host RAM.

Updated 2026-09-16. The numbers below are from the live five-GPU server logs in `results/prefix-audit-20260916/`.

## Current status

- 40 backbone layers and 384 experts are distributed across GPUs `2,0,1,3,4` with EP shards `77,77,77,77,76`.
- **1,000,000-Token Prefill Demonstrated**: Full 1M context cold prefill is empirically verified and benchmarked on 4× A100 80GB (`cuda:0,1,2,3`) using 4-stage Chunked Pipeline Parallelism and head-accumulated BMM indexer with zero OOM errors.
- **CED (Causal Encoder-Decoder) / Decoder SWA Bounded Replay**: Intermediate prefill chunks run exclusively through layers 0..20 (Encoder side), generating all global compressed KV and candidate index representations. Decoder layers 21..39 only process the final 128-token SWA window, saving **~47% of prefill compute** on long contexts.
- **In-GPU Slot Cache & Prefix Replay**: Consecutive requests sharing a common prefix (e.g. Claude Code tool use / agentic coding) detect Longest Common Prefix (LCP) in GPU VRAM across active slots (`copy_seq`), forwarding only suffix tokens (e.g. 500 suffix tokens in 2s vs re-prefilling 128K tokens in 15 minutes). The web dashboard clearly distinguishes **Cold Prefill** from **Prefix Replay** with live hit rate and instant ETA.
- **Compacted Canonical Snapshot Storage**: Host-RAM snapshots deduplicate multi-device GPU mirrors into a single canonical copy per owner, bound SWA windows to 128 rows, and slice Engram history to logical prefix length, slashing host RAM footprint by ~75% and accelerating restore via fast P2P GPU broadcast.
- **Jev Mode Implemented**: Parallel non-autoregressive structured output engine with hierarchical persistent GPU prefix caching (`JevPrefixTree`). Replaces serial autoregressive JSON decode with parallel candidate log-probability scoring, achieving up to **2,854× speedup** on 30-field extraction (24 ms) and 100% schema consistency with zero output decode tokens.
- Prefix snapshots, multi-anchor reuse, and continuation block replay are implemented.
- DSpark/MTP draft and verification are implemented and verified with `--mtp 5 --mtp-device 4`.
- For prompts over `DSV41_MTP_LONG_PROMPT_LIMIT`, the server can unload DSpark and fall back to ordinary decode. This reduces MTP memory pressure but does not remove the full-context cache limit.

## Deployment Profiles & Usage Recipes

DeepSeek-V4.1 supports flexible deployment profiles tailored to specific production workloads—ranging from ultra-low latency, multi-agent interactive coding to 1,000,000-token full-repository analysis.

### Deployment Profiles & Trade-Off Comparison

| **⚡ Speed & Multi-Agent** | Claude Code, interactive chat, parallel tool calls | **64K** (65,536) | **4 Slots** (`5`) | **50–55 tok/s** | **80–120 tok/s** | **12–16 GiB** | Bounds context to 64K to free VRAM; expands concurrency to 4 parallel decode streams | [`./run_speed_agent.sh`](file:///mnt/ssdraid/git/deepseekv4.1/run_speed_agent.sh) |

from __future__ import annotations

import ctypes
import hashlib
import os
import subprocess

import torch

HERE = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
NVCC = os.environ.get("DSV41_NVCC", "/usr/local/cuda-12.8/bin/nvcc")
_cuda = ctypes.CDLL("libcuda.so.1")
_modules: dict[tuple[str, int], ctypes.c_void_p] = {}
_funcs: dict[tuple[str, int], ctypes.c_void_p] = {}


def _check(err, what):
    if err != 0:
        raise RuntimeError(f"{what} failed with CUDA error {err}")


def _cubin(src_name: str) -> bytes:
    src = os.path.join(HERE, "cuda", src_name)
    code = open(src, "rb").read()
    tag = hashlib.sha1(code).hexdigest()[:12]
    out = os.path.join(HERE, "cuda", f".{src_name}.{tag}.sm80.cubin")
    if not os.path.exists(out):
        subprocess.run([NVCC, "-cubin", "-arch=sm_80", "-O3", "-o", out, src], check=True)
    return open(out, "rb").read()


def get_function(src_name: str, func: str, device: torch.device) -> ctypes.c_void_p:
    key = (src_name, device.index)
    if key not in _modules:
        with torch.cuda.device(device):
            torch.cuda.current_stream()  # make sure the context exists
            image = _cubin(src_name)
            mod = ctypes.c_void_p()
            _check(_cuda.cuModuleLoadData(ctypes.byref(mod), image), "cuModuleLoadData")
            _modules[key] = mod
    fkey = (src_name + ":" + func, device.index)
    if fkey not in _funcs:
        f = ctypes.c_void_p()
        _check(_cuda.cuModuleGetFunction(ctypes.byref(f), _modules[key], func.encode()), "cuModuleGetFunction")
        _funcs[fkey] = f
    return _funcs[fkey]


def launch(func, grid, block, args, device: torch.device, shared: int = 0):
    """args: list of ctypes values (c_void_p for pointers)."""
    ptrs = (ctypes.c_void_p * len(args))(*[ctypes.cast(ctypes.pointer(a), ctypes.c_void_p) for a in args])
    with torch.cuda.device(device):  # the module handle belongs to this device's primary context
        stream = torch.cuda.current_stream(device).cuda_stream
        _check(_cuda.cuLaunchKernel(func, grid[0], grid[1], grid[2], block[0], block[1], block[2], shared,
                                    ctypes.c_void_p(stream), ptrs, None), "cuLaunchKernel")

I cloned the repo and diffed its kernel inventory against ours (`src/c/vkernels/kernels`, `torch_ops`, `comm`). Context: that repo is a **sm80/A100, single-process, CUDA-graph-centric runtime** for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash — hand-written CUDA launched via the driver API, FP8 dense weights + FP4 MoE experts. Here's what it has that we don't, ranked by how much I'd want to steal:

## Real gaps — kernels we don't have anywhere

**1. FP8/FP4 weight-only *tensor-core* GEMMs for sm80 (`fp8_tc.cu`, `fp8_tcw.cu`, `fp8_tcg.cu`, `fp4_tc.cu`, `fp4_tcw.cu`)**
We have this story on CDNA/HIP (`moe_fused.hip`, `glm_fp8_block_gemv` split-K) and in Triton (`v41_fp8_gemm`, `v41_mxfp4_gemv`), but **no CUDA/mma implementation** — on NVIDIA our quantized paths fall back to Triton. These kernels are the reference for how to do it on Ampere/Hopper:
- **Register-level decode**: `e4m3x4→bf16` via `prmt` bit tricks and `e2m1x8→bf16` with the E8M0 scale folded in as a `bf16x2 fma` — zero LUT/smem round-trip, exact same numbers as dequant-then-cuBLAS.
- **The `PERM_K` weight layout trick** (`w8.py`): weight bytes of each 16-k group stored as `0,1,8,9,2,3,10,11,…` so `ldmatrix` hands each lane its mma A fragment pre-arranged for decode. Weights are permuted once at load; every kernel then reads the same layout.
- **Split-K with an atomic-counter "last block does the reduce" epilogue** — same idea as our `gemv_decode_fp8_splitk` but as a full GEMM family (M≤16, M≤64, tiled M≥32 with 4-stage `cp.async` + `ldmatrix`).
- **`group_cols` block-diagonal mode** in `fp8_tcg.cu`: the o-projection's block-diagonal structure fused into the GEMM's row indexing, avoiding a separate gather/scatter.

**2. Grouped GEMV with pair-list dispatch, no atomics (`fp4_gemv_pairs`)**
One output per (pair, n), activation staged in shared memory **transposed** (`xs[j][c]`) so the 32 lanes read consecutive addresses — no bank conflicts, and expert/row/weight read from index arrays so the grouped decode GEMV needs zero pre-sorting of weights. Our `v41_mxfp4_gemv` is a straightforward Triton GEMV without this staging or the no-atomics pair layout.

**3. Small/large group kernel pairing for grouped MoE**
`fp4_tc` handles groups ≤16 tokens (expert re-read per 16-token tile); `fp4_tcw` flips the operands — weights as the mma A-operand — so a group of up to 64 tokens **reads the expert once**, with `cp.async`-pipelined activation tiles, and the launcher routes each group to the right kernel by token count (skipping other GPUs' EP shards with a zero-fill mode). Our `moe_fused` has one fixed schedule; this adaptive split is a cheap win for decode-shaped EP loads.

**4. Push-style one-shot all-reduce for small vectors (`allreduce.cu`)**
Our `comm/allreduce` is ring (bandwidth-optimal, latency-poor). This one is three tiny graph-capturable kernels (`ar_push` P2P stores into a per-peer buffer, `ar_signal` fence+flag spin, `ar_reduce` sum) sized for decode-token vectors, no NCCL, works inside a captured graph. A natural complement to `pipeline_boundary` for decode-step collectives.

**5. Device-side EP messaging kernels (`p2p.cu`)**
`p2p_copy_row` (scatter rows to per-token destination slots + sequence) and `p2p_sum_rows` — the mechanism that lets the whole EP token step run as one CUDA graph per GPU with no host round trips. We have `kv_scatter`/`p2p_gather` for the KV path but not this token-dispatch row-scatter + flag-wait pattern.

**6. Fused act+quant epilogues (`fused.py`: `swiglu_quant`, `norm_quant`, `hc_pre_norm_quant2`)**
SwiGLU (with clamp) + FP8 quant + optional 8-row mma permutation in **one** pass; RMSNorm + quant fused. We explicitly pay a round-trip for this today — `aiter_ops.py` applies the clamp-swiglu in torch *between* GEMM stages because aiter's in-kernel SwiGLU can't express the clamp. These are directly portable Triton and remove a full read+write of the intermediate.

## Worth copying as *patterns*, not kernels

- **`cukern.py` launcher**: runtime `nvcc -cubin` + `ctypes` `cuModuleLoadData`/`cuLaunchKernel`. No torch extension build, works with any torch, graph-capture safe. Nice for shipping experimental NVIDIA kernels without touching our CMake/pybind machinery.
- **`sparse_attn_decode_split`**: split-KV partial softmax (`pm/pl/pacc`) + combine kernel for sparse decode over long contexts — our `v41_sparse_attention` has the online-softmax core but not the split-and-combine variant for large `n_kv`.

## Probably *not* worth taking

The higher-level machinery (Jev structured-output scoring, in-GPU prefix replay, CED/SWA-bounded prefill) is runtime/serving design, not kernels — interesting to read, out of our layer. And the hyper-connection kernels (`hc_pre/hc_post/sinkhorn`) duplicate what our `mhc_*`/`glm_mhc_mix` already cover.

**Caveat**: everything there is sm80-specific (`mma.m16n8k16`, `cp.async`, P2P within one process). Our primary targets are CDNA — so the port is *algorithm/schedule* transfer (PERM_K-style layout, register decode, operand-flip, push-AR, fused epilogues) with MFMA equivalents, except items 4–6, which are nearly portable as-is.

Want me to start with one of these — I'd suggest the fused `swiglu_quant`/`norm_quant` epilogues (pure Triton, lowest effort, kills a known round-trip in `aiter_ops`) or an sm80 CUDA port of the fp8 tensor-core GEMM family?

## Ranking by (verified win × portability ÷ effort)

**1. Fused quant epilogues — do this first** (`dsv41-fused-quant-epilogues.md`, 185 lines)
Strongest plan of the six. Quantified: stage-split swiglu pays 105 MB/layer eager, 54.7 MB with our Triton op → **21.1 MB fused (−61% to −80%)**; W4A4 act-scratch round-trip −74%. Pure Triton in `torch_ops`, no MFMA, numerics proven bit-identical given exact ceil-log2/div_rn/rint (one ≤1-ulp fork to contract-gate: silu-rounding order). Directly kills the `aiter_ops` stage-split round-trip. Caveat it flags honestly: decode intermediates fit MI300A's 256 MB L2, so the real test is prefill.

**2. FP8/FP4 tensor-core GEMM family** (`dsv41-tc-gemm-family.md`, 256 lines)
Best-extracted reference material: PERM_K layout, prmt decode, split-K self-resetting counters (our `gemm_bf16_splitk_fused` already prototypes the same epilogue), `group_cols` block-diagonal o-proj. Bonus finding: MI300A has **native fp8 MFMA** (`mfma_f32_16x16x32_fp8`, already used in our `dsa.hip`) with UE8M0 accumulator scaling — can skip decode entirely; A/B it against the decode-port. Order: transcribe `fp8_tc.cu` (157 lines) → HIP port → grouped fp4. Top risk: fn vs fnuz fp8 2× silent mismatch.

**3. Push one-shot allreduce** (`dsv41-push-allreduce.md`, 219 lines)
Clean fit: slots into `classify_boundary` (`kSameNodePeer` → push, cross-node → RCCL), host oracle over `MockChannel` keeps GPU-less tests, 3 kernels capture verbatim vs RCCL's 1. Port near-verbatim to xGMI. Risks: lockstep-replay deadlock, device `seq` across re-captures.

**4. FP4 pair-list GEMV** (`dsv41-fp4-gemv-pairs.md`, 68 lines)
Worth porting for decode only — portable by class (LDS+FMA+shuffle, 20 KB smem vs 64 KB available). One nice catch: it's *more accurate* than our bf16-rounded oracle, so parity must be tolerance-based, not bit-exact. Integration via our existing `Tunable(..., persists=True)` pattern.

**5. P2P EP dispatch** (`dsv41-p2p-ep-dispatch.md`, 361 lines)
Confirmed real gap (peer-destination scatter + device flag sync + device sum-combine — we have none of the three), and the doc doubles as a capture-rules codification. But biggest scope: new `comm/ep_dispatch` module, ~4 kernels + mailbox + host model. Highest value for a future EP runtime, not a quick win.

**6. Group-split routing — demoted** (`dsv41-group-split-routing.md`, 167 lines)
The Monte-Carlo verdict is that this is **mostly not worth it**: at decode (M ≤ 128, top-k 8, EP/5) group sizes essentially never exceed 16, so the operand-flipped cap-64 kernel saves *zero* HBM bytes — crossover is M ≳ 500. Only real value is skew insurance (4× traffic cut on all-pairs-hit-one-expert). Recommendation: instrument group-size dispatch (kill-switched) and gate adoption on skewed traffic; port the flipped kernel last, if ever.

"""Consolidated benchmark of the dsv41 A100 kernels vs bf16 cuBLAS baselines.

Runs on one A100. Sweeps decode-realistic shapes for:
  - fp8_gemv      (M<=16 weight-only fp8 GEMV)
  - fp8_gemm_tc   (tensor-core dispatch: fp8_tc / fp8_tcw / fp8_tcg)
  - fp4_gemv_pairs(grouped E2M1 decode GEMV, pair-list, no atomics)
  - fp4 tc/tcw    (grouped E2M1 tensor-core GEMM, small/large groups)
  - bf16 cuBLAS baselines for each (weights dequantized to bf16)

Every kernel is parity-checked against a fp32 reference before timing
(exact decode + fp32 accumulation => tight tolerance).

Writes results to bench_dsv41_results.json (shape, kernel, us, GB/s, TFLOP/s).
"""
import json
import os
import sys
import time

import torch

sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)) + "/dsv41")
from dsv41 import cukern  # noqa: E402
from dsv41.quant import dequant_fp8_block, dequant_fp4, fake_quant_fp8  # noqa: E402
from dsv41.w8 import permute_k  # noqa: E402

dev = torch.device("cuda:0")
torch.manual_seed(0)
RESULTS = []


def bench(fn, iters=50, warmup=5):
    for _ in range(warmup):
        fn()
    torch.cuda.synchronize(dev)
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(iters):
        fn()
    torch.cuda.synchronize(dev)
    return (time.perf_counter() - t0) / iters


def rand_fp8(N, K):
    w = torch.randint(0, 256, (N, K), device=dev, dtype=torch.uint8)
    w[(w & 0x7F) == 0x7F] = 0  # no NaN codes
    s = torch.randint(110, 130, ((N + 31) // 32, K // 32), device=dev, dtype=torch.uint8)
    return w, s


def gb(N, K, bytes_per_weight, M=1):
    # weights + scales + activations + output, single pass
    return (N * K * bytes_per_weight + N * K / 32 + M * K * 2 + M * N * 4) / 1e9

  - fp4_gemm_tc   (grouped E2M1 tensor-core GEMM, fp4_tc/fp4_tcw dispatch)

import time

from dsv41.w8 import permute_k  # noqa: E402

def bench(fn, iters=50, warmup=5):

    torch.cuda.synchronize(dev)
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(iters):

    torch.cuda.synchronize(dev)

print("== fp4_gemm_tc (fp4_tc/fp4_tcw dispatch) ==", flush=True)
E2, I2, H2 = 64, 2048, 7168  # K % 128 == 0 required

    n_pairs = M * topk
    w13 = torch.randint(0, 256, (E2, 2 * I2, H2 // 2), device=dev, dtype=torch.uint8)

    pair_tok_s = pair_tok[order].to(torch.int32)

"""Isolate the fp4_gemm_tc parity NaN: uniform groups (repo-test style) vs variable groups."""
import os
import sys

import torch

sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)) + "/dsv41")
from dsv41 import cukern  # noqa: E402
from dsv41.quant import dequant_fp4, fake_quant_fp8  # noqa: E402

dev = torch.device("cuda:0")
torch.manual_seed(0)


def check(tag, xp, w, s, grp_expert, grp_start, pair_tok, n_pairs, max_tokens, x, wb_all):
    y = cukern.fp4_gemm_tc(xp, w, s, grp_expert, grp_start, pair_tok, n_pairs, max_tokens)
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    bad = []
    for p in range(n_pairs):
        ref = x[int(pair_tok[p])].float() @ wb_all[int(grp_expert[p])].float().T
        e = ((y[p] - ref).abs().max() / ref.abs().max()).item()
        if e > 1e-2 or e != e:
            bad.append((p, int(grp_expert[p]), int(grp_start[int(grp_expert[p] == grp_expert).nonzero()[0]]) if False else 0, e))
    nan_rows = int(torch.isnan(y).any(dim=1).sum())
    print(f"{tag}: nan_rows={nan_rows}/{n_pairs} bad={len(bad)} first5={bad[:5]}", flush=True)
    return y


# --- case 1: repo-test style, uniform groups
E, N, K = 8, 4608, 5120
w = torch.randint(0, 256, (E, N, K // 2), device=dev, dtype=torch.uint8)
s = torch.randint(112, 128, (E, N, K // 32), device=dev, dtype=torch.uint8)
wb_all = torch.stack([dequant_fp4(w[e], s[e]) for e in range(E)])

    x = fake_quant_fp8(torch.randn(M, K, device=dev, dtype=torch.bfloat16) * 2, 32)
    xp = cukern.permute_x(x)
    experts = torch.arange(G, device=dev, dtype=torch.int32)
    grp_start = torch.arange(0, G * M + 1, M, device=dev, dtype=torch.int32)
    pair_tok = torch.arange(M, device=dev, dtype=torch.int32).repeat(G)
    check(f"uniform G={G} M={M}", xp, w, s, experts, grp_start, pair_tok, G * M, M, x, wb_all)

# --- case 2: variable groups, random pairs, E=64 N=4096 K=7168

s2 = torch.randint(110, 135, (E2, N2, K2 // 32), device=dev, dtype=torch.uint8)
wb_all2 = torch.stack([dequant_fp4(w2[e], s2[e]) for e in range(E2)])
for M in (16, 64):
    topk = 8
    n_pairs = M * topk
    x = fake_quant_fp8(torch.randn(M, K2, device=dev, dtype=torch.bfloat16) * 2, 32)
    pair_tok = torch.randint(0, M, (n_pairs,), device=dev, dtype=torch.int32)
    expert = torch.randint(0, E2, (n_pairs,), device=dev, dtype=torch.int32)
    order = torch.argsort(expert)
    expert_s = expert[order].to(torch.int32)
    pair_tok_s = pair_tok[order].to(torch.int32)
    grp_expert, grp_start, counts = [], [0], []
    i = 0
    while i < n_pairs:
        e = int(expert_s[i])
        j = i
        while j < n_pairs and int(expert_s[j]) == e and (j - i) < 64:
            j += 1
        grp_expert.append(e)
        counts.append(j - i)
        grp_start.append(j)
        i = j
    grp_expert_t = torch.tensor(grp_expert, device=dev, dtype=torch.int32)
    grp_start_t = torch.tensor(grp_start + [n_pairs], device=dev, dtype=torch.int32)
    xp = cukern.permute_x(x)
    print(f"variable M={M}: G={len(grp_expert)} counts[min,max]=[{min(counts)},{max(counts)}]", flush=True)
    check(f"variable M={M}", xp, w2, s2, grp_expert_t, grp_start_t, pair_tok_s, n_pairs, 64, x, wb_all2)

# --- case 3: variable but all chunks exactly 8 (tc8 path only)
for chunk in (8, 16, 64):
    M, n_pairs = 64, 64 * 8
    x = fake_quant_fp8(torch.randn(M, K2, device=dev, dtype=torch.bfloat16) * 2, 32)
    pair_tok = torch.randint(0, M, (n_pairs,), device=dev, dtype=torch.int32)
    expert = torch.randint(0, E2, (n_pairs,), device=dev, dtype=torch.int32)
    order = torch.argsort(expert)
    expert_s = expert[order].to(torch.int32)
    pair_tok_s = pair_tok[order].to(torch.int32)
    grp_expert, grp_start = [], [0]
    i = 0
    while i < n_pairs:
        e = int(expert_s[i])
        j = min(i + chunk, n_pairs)
        # ensure same expert within chunk: fill remainder with this expert's other pairs is complex;
        # instead chunk by count per expert
        grp_expert.append(e)
        grp_start.append(j)
        i = j
    # NOTE: chunks may span experts here; if NaN persists only in this case, chunking isn't the issue
    grp_expert_t = torch.tensor(grp_expert, device=dev, dtype=torch.int32)
    grp_start_t = torch.tensor(grp_start + [n_pairs], device=dev, dtype=torch.int32)
    xp = cukern.permute_x(x)
    check(f"chunk={chunk} (mixed-expert chunks!)", xp, w2, s2, grp_expert_t, grp_start_t, pair_tok_s, n_pairs, chunk, x, wb_all2)

All four kernel families are now benchmarked on a real A100 (nid002280/332, 80GB SXM, CUDA 12.6, torch 2.6+cu124). Full sweep done after fixing three bugs in my harness (absolute-vs-relative parity, bf16 scale-overflow in the fp4 TC path with `s≥129`, graph-based timing to remove launch overhead). Results saved to `docs/candidates/dsv41-a100-bench-results.json`.

## What the A100 numbers say

**fp8_gemm_tc — the clear winner, and it beats the hand GEMV even at M=1**

| shape | fp8_gemm_tc | fp8_gemv (hand) | bf16 cuBLAS |
|---|---|---|---|
| M=1, 512×5120 | **6.8 µs** (402 GB/s) | 32.8 µs | 8.6 µs |
| M=1, 5120×2304 | **11.7 µs** (1038 GB/s) | 25.9 µs | 13.4 µs |
| M=4, 5120×8192 | **36.2 µs** | — | 58.5 µs |
| M=16, 4608×5120 | **28.3 µs** | — | 33.6 µs |
| M=32, 5120×7168 | **46.7 µs** | — | 56.0 µs |
| M=64/128 | 57.8/68.6 µs | — | **35.1/33.1 µs** (cuBLAS wins) |
| group_cols o-proj (8×8192×4096) | **27.8 µs** | — | 48.3 µs |

Sweet spot is exactly M≤32 (memory-bound regime): 1.2–2.0× over cuBLAS plus half the weight bytes. At M≥64 the register-decode path falls behind dense bf16 TC. The `group_cols` block-diagonal mode is a big win (1.7×) — directly relevant to our attention o-proj.

**fp8_gemv (the hand GEMV) — don't port it.** 25–33 µs, 83–472 GB/s, latency-bound on this machine (few blocks at M=1). Its own TC path beats it 3–5×. This downgrades that part of the `tc-gemm-family` candidate: transcribe the TC kernels, skip `fp8_gemv.cu`.

**fp4 grouped: TC path dominates the pair-list GEMV at every M** (same M×topk work):

| M tokens | fp4_gemv_pairs | fp4_gemm_tc |
|---|---|---|
| 16 | 1851 µs | **907 µs** |
| 64 | 7366 µs | **1145 µs** |
| 256 | — | 1611 µs (74.6 TFLOP/s) |

The pair-list GEMV also only hits 617–775 GB/s (re-reads weights per pair) — well under A100 HBM. This is a real design-pivot signal for our `fp4-gemv-pairs` candidate doc: on sm80, the grouped TC kernels (`fp4_tc/fp4_tcw` with grp_start offsets, ≤64 tokens/group, variable group sizes supported) are strictly better. Worth a HIP/MI300 comparison later since MI300A has native fp8 MFMA but *not* fp4.

## Cluster notes
- Working recipe: `#SBATCH --uenv=prgenv-gnu/24.11:v1 --view=modules` (nvcc 12.6.2) + torch 2.6+cu124 venv at `/iopsstor/scratch/cscs/xyao/dsv41-probe/venv`. Queue was empty today — jobs start in ~2 min.
- One caveat found: the fp4 TC kernels require E8M0 scales `s ≤ 128` (they fold `2^(s-1)` in bf16; `s≥129` → inf). Real checkpoints satisfy this; worth a note in the port docs as a contract.
